topic: Antibiotic prescribing for respiratory tract infection

audits.title: Medical audit changes physicians' prescribing of antibiotics for respiratory tract infections.
audits.standard: Audit Project Odense model for respiratory tract infection prescribing

cycle1.result: 45% of patients did not receive an antibiotic in the intervention group.

audits.intervention: Active intervention between registrations (feedback and follow-up discussion).

cycle2.result: 55% did not receive an antibiotic in the intervention group.

audits.other_findings: 25 physicians served as controls; the proportion not receiving antibiotics rose in both groups.
audits.citation: Melander E, Björgell A, Björgell P, Ovhed I, Mölstad S. Medical audit changes physicians' prescribing of antibiotics for respiratory tract infections. Scand J Prim Health Care. 1999;17(3):180-184. doi:10.1080/028134399750002610. PMID: 10555249.

audits.title: Long-lasting improvement in general practitioners' prescribing of antibiotics by means of medical audit.
audits.standard: Recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of respiratory infections (APO method)
audits.setting: 24 Danish GPs with Audit Project Odense and Department of Clinical Microbiology, Odense University Hospital
audits.intervention: Courses, visits to the laboratory and distribution of recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of respiratory infections.

cycle2.result: Penicillin/broad-spectrum ratio 2.70 (1.94 in 1993), significantly higher increase than in controls.

audits.other_findings: Reduction in antibiotic prescriptions was matched by controls; changes were maintained after education stopped.
audits.citation: Munck AP, Gahrn-Hansen B, Søgaard P, Søgaard J. Long-lasting improvement in general practitioners' prescribing of antibiotics by means of medical audit. Scand J Prim Health Care. 1999;17(3):185-190. doi:10.1080/028134399750002629. PMID: 10555250.

audits.title: Audit of management of respiratory infections among children.
audits.standard: Checklist and scoring system for structure and process of acute respiratory infection care
audits.setting: Two large Primary Health Care Centres, Abha, Asir region

cycle1.result: Antibiotics were the commonest drugs prescribed; fewer than one third of files had appropriate recording of history and examination.

audits.other_findings: Inadequate structures in both centres; continuing education and community health education recommended.
audits.citation: Al-Khaldi YM, Al-Sharif AI, Gilban KS, Al-Jaser AO, Al-Hamami QM. Audit of management of respiratory infections among children. Saudi Med J. 2001;22(3):244-248. PMID: 11307111.

audits.title: Respiratory tract infections in Greenland: results of an audit project.
audits.standard: Audit Project Odense (APO) method, compared with Danish practice
audits.setting: District health services along the Greenland coast (25 district medical officers, nine districts)

cycle1.result: Lung infections 26%, throat 22%, otitis media 16%; paraclinical tests in 32%; antibiotics in 47%, two-thirds penicillin V.

audits.other_findings: Fewer tests and more antibiotics than in Denmark.
audits.citation: Gahm-Hansen B, Aaen-Larsen B, Mosgaard L, Damsgaard J, Munck A. Respiratory tract infections in Greenland: results of an audit project. Int J Circumpolar Health. 2004;63 Suppl 2:209-213. doi:10.3402/ijch.v63i0.17904. PMID: 15736654.

audits.title: Effect of standard treatment guidelines with or without prescription audit on prescribing for acute respiratory tract infection (ARI) and diarrhoea in some thana health complexes (THCs) of Bangladesh.
audits.standard: Standard treatment guidelines for acute respiratory infection

cycle1.result: 38 of 60 health complexes did not comply with STG for ARI (unnecessary antibiotics in >50% of encounters); 26 prescribed antibiotics in >=72% of encounters.

audits.intervention: Standard treatment guidelines with prescription audit (group I) or guidelines alone (group II), with a control group

cycle2.result: Antibiotic use fell by 23.7% of encounters with STG plus audit and 15.2% with STG alone; 15.2% and 6.9% after adjusting for control.

audits.other_findings: Diarrhoea was dropped from the intervention as most prescribers used ORS.
audits.citation: Chowdhury AK, Khan OF, Matin MA, Begum K, Galib MA. Effect of standard treatment guidelines with or without prescription audit on prescribing for acute respiratory tract infection (ARI) and diarrhoea in some thana health complexes (THCs) of Bangladesh. Bangladesh Med Res Counc Bull. 2007;33(1):21-30. PMID: 18246731.

audits.title: Point prevalence audit surveys of respiratory tract infection consultations and antibiotic prescribing in primary care before and during the COVID-19 pandemic in Ireland.
audits.setting: General practices in Ireland (point prevalence audit surveys, part of a European study)

cycle1.result: Antibiotics prescribed in 54% of RTI consultations

cycle2.result: Antibiotics prescribed in 21% of RTI consultations (23% in March-May 2020)

audits.other_findings: 765 consultations in total; bronchitis and tonsillitis consultations led to antibiotics in 67% and 85%; point-of-care testing used in less than 1%. The fall in prescribing followed the COVID-19 pandemic, not a planned intervention.
audits.citation: Shah M, Fleming A, Barbosa TM, van der Velden AW, Parveen S, Vellinga A. Point prevalence audit surveys of respiratory tract infection consultations and antibiotic prescribing in primary care before and during the COVID-19 pandemic in Ireland. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2023;78(5):1270-1277. doi:10.1093/jac/dkad088. PMID: 36974983.

audits.title: Disease-Specific Quality Indicators for Outpatient Antibiotic Prescribing for Respiratory Infections (ESAC Quality Indicators) Applied to Point Prevalence Audit Surveys in General Practices in 13 European Countries.
audits.standard: ESAC quality indicators, e.g. bronchitis in adults ≤30% antibiotics; acute upper RTI <20%; tonsillitis and sinusitis 0-20%; pneumonia in adults 90-100%
audits.setting: General practices in 13 European countries (point prevalence audit study)

cycle1.result: Antibiotic prescribed in 30% of consultations; tonsillitis 69%; bronchitis indicator met only in Denmark and Spain

cycle2.result: Antibiotic prescribed in 16% of consultations; tonsillitis 75%, exceeding the indicator in all countries

audits.other_findings: Upper RTI target met in most countries except Ireland (both surveys), Croatia (PPAS-1) and Greece (PPAS-4); pneumonia prescribing was below 90-100% in most countries.
audits.citation: Vellinga A, Luke-Currier A, Garzón-Orjuela N, Aabenhus R, Anastasaki M, Balan A, et al.. Disease-Specific Quality Indicators for Outpatient Antibiotic Prescribing for Respiratory Infections (ESAC Quality Indicators) Applied to Point Prevalence Audit Surveys in General Practices in 13 European Countries. Antibiotics (Basel). 2023;12(3):572. doi:10.3390/antibiotics12030572. PMID: 36978439.

audits.title: [Respiratory tract infections in general practice--the effect of a medical audit project].
audits.standard: Prescribe antibiotics only when necessary and use penicillin when an antibiotic is indicated (local recommendations)
audits.intervention: Courses, visits to clinical microbiology department and distribution of diagnosis and treatment recommendations
audits.other_findings: Group A streptococcal testing in tonsillitis was used more often in 1993.

audits.title: Operationalising outpatient antimicrobial stewardship to reduce system-wide antibiotics for acute bronchitis.
audits.standard: Guidelines recommending no antibiotics for acute uncomplicated bronchitis; aim to reduce antibiotic prescribing from 65% to <32% by April 2020
audits.setting: 18 community-based outpatient clinics, VA Tennessee Valley Healthcare System

cycle1.period: July to December 2018 (6 months before intervention)
cycle1.result: Antibiotics prescribed in 314 of 486 (64.6%) acute bronchitis/URI encounters; 667 of 1054 (63%) over January to December 2018.

audits.intervention: Seven PDSA cycles: provider needs-assessment interviews; CDC patient education materials and supportive care prescription pads; individual comparative feedback emails; individualised focused case reviews with high prescribers; primary care grand rounds.

cycle2.result: Antibiotics prescribed in 154 of 418 (36.8%) encounters (p=0.002 across periods).

audits.other_findings: The target of <32% was not reached; feedback emails were high effort with low read rates, while case reviews of 14 high prescribers gave the largest reduction. No change in return visits or calls; VA clinics improved more than contract clinics.
audits.citation: Johnson MC, Hulgan T, Cooke RG, Kleinpell R, Roumie C, Callaway-Lane C, et al.. Operationalising outpatient antimicrobial stewardship to reduce system-wide antibiotics for acute bronchitis. BMJ Open Qual. 2021;10(3):e001275. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2020-001275. PMID: 34210668.
